summary: This informational document defines a reference framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance in TRILL networks. It focuses on fault and performance management.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7174 is a plan for the tools a network operator uses to check a TRILL network: does it still work, and is it fast enough. It says where the checking software sits in each switch, what the checks are called, and how a test packet has to be shaped so that it travels the same path as the traffic it is testing.

questions: how do you monitor trill networks
how do you find faults in trill
subtitle: A framework for checking whether a TRILL network is broken, slow, or working.

tldr.problem: A TRILL network has to be checked for faults and measured for performance, but TRILL behaves differently from ordinary Ethernet bridging in ways that make the standard bridge tools a poor fit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out a reference framework: where the OAM layer sits relative to link checks and to customer-facing checks, the domains and endpoints the checks run between, and the frame format that lets a check follow exactly the same path as real traffic.
tldr.outcome: The document is a framework, not a protocol. It gives the shape of the solution and the configuration parameters, and leaves the actual message formats to later documents.

today: RFC 7174 is an Informational RFC published in May 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a reference framework for TRILL OAM: it fixes the shape of the solution and the configuration parameters, while the specific message formats and mechanisms are left to other documents.

sections.title: What the Document Covers
sections.content:
The document specifies a reference framework for Operations, Administration, and Maintenance in TRILL networks. TRILL itself is a protocol for shortest-path frame routing in multi-hop networks with arbitrary topologies and link technologies, using the IS-IS routing protocol, and the devices that implement it are called TRILL Switches or RBridges.

Four properties of TRILL make it different from ordinary Ethernet bridging, and they matter for monitoring. A TRILL network can use any link technology between its switches, so a port might not even have a 48-bit MAC address and could instead be identified by an IP address or not at all. TRILL does not enforce that the unicast path and the multicast path between a pair of switches are the same. It does not impose symmetry between the forward and reverse paths. And TRILL switches terminate spanning tree protocols rather than propagating them.

Within OAM, the Operations part is about finding problems that stop the network working, and about watching for problems before they happen. Administration is keeping track of network resources. Maintenance is about repairs, upgrades and preventive work. The ISO standard for network management divides this into five areas, commonly called FCAPS: fault management, configuration management, accounting management, performance management and security management. This document focuses on the first and fourth, fault management and performance management, which map onto the Operations and Maintenance parts of OAM.

What follows is a generic framework for a comprehensive solution meeting the requirements in the earlier requirements document. The specific mechanisms are out of scope, and later documents are expected to cover the optional reporting of errors in TRILL user traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL is not ordinary Ethernet, so the usual bridge tools do not fit it. This RFC sets out what a monitoring system for TRILL has to look like, and leaves the detail of the messages for later.

sections.title: The OAM Model
sections.content:
The TRILL layer is independent of the underlying link technology, so TRILL can run over anything that carries TRILL packets, such as Ethernet, PPP or IP. TRILL offers a virtual Ethernet service that is transparent to everything above it, and TRILL OAM observes that strict layering. The layering of interest is with BFD, which is typically used for fast failure detection, with Ethernet Connectivity Fault Management on paths from an external device, over a TRILL campus, to another external device, and with link-level OAM on the links inside the campus, which depends on the link technology.

Connectivity Fault Management can act as a client-layer mechanism, giving the customer end-to-end fault management over the campus, with the edge ports of the TRILL network visible to it through the optional presence of an intermediate point in the edge ports, or as a transport-layer mechanism, giving fault management for the bridged LANs that interconnect TRILL switches. One-hop BFD runs between adjacent switches and gives fast link and node failure detection; because it also exercises part of the TRILL protocol stack, it sits a layer above link OAM. The two differ in an important way: a BFD transmitter is always bound to one specific output port, and can send to a neighbour even while the adjacency is still being set up, whereas TRILL OAM messages are typically sent as though they had been received on an input port, so the routing function chooses the output ports and will only use links that are up and already in the local view of the campus.

Work can be done at three levels of detail. Network OAM works in a test VLAN or fine-grained label that reaches every TRILL switch, and uses test flows, both unicast and multicast, so that all the paths are covered. Service OAM works in the real VLAN or label set that end stations actually use. Flow OAM works on individual end-station flows, and while it is the most precise it poses scalability problems if applied to large numbers of flows.

The pieces that the functions run between are the maintenance entities. An entity defines a relationship between two points in the network where OAM functions are applied, and those two points are maintenance end points. A set of end points belonging to the same maintenance domain is a maintenance association, and between the end points there can be zero or more maintenance intermediate points. The end points are the active part: they send the messages and they make sure the messages do not leak out of the domain, for example out of the TRILL network and into end stations. The intermediate points are internal to the domain and mostly passive: they forward messages and answer some of them. A maintenance domain is a collection of TRILL switches whose faults and performance degradation are managed by one operator. Since TRILL runs in a single IS-IS area with a single operator, one default domain is normally enough. When several TRILL networks are interconnected, domains must either be disjoint or nested, and a nested domain must be given a lower level number than the domain that encloses it, so that the higher domain sees the lower one as a single hop.
sections.plainLanguage: Checks run between pairs of points, and the points in between help pass the messages along. The RFC also divides the work up: checking the whole network, checking one service, or checking one flow.

sections.title: The OAM Frame
sections.content:
For an OAM message to test the data path accurately, it has to be transparent to the switches it passes through. It must be indistinguishable from an ordinary TRILL data packet during normal processing, and only the switch it is aimed at should recognise and trap it as a control message. Methods are also needed to stop OAM packets from being sent out as native frames.

The frame format puts the link header first, then the initial 6-byte fixed part of the TRILL header, then any TRILL header extensions, then a fixed-size flow entropy field, then a 2-byte OAM Ethertype, then the OAM message channel, and finally the link trailer. The TRILL header, link header and link trailer should be as similar as practical to those of the real data packet the check is testing. The OAM Ethertype marks the boundary between the flow entropy and the message channel, and sits at a predictable offset from the TRILL header so that applications can find the start of the channel. The link trailer is usually a checksum such as the Ethernet frame check sequence.

The flow entropy field is filled with real or synthetic data that imitates the flow being tested. It always begins with the destination and source MAC address area and then the data label area. For a layer 2 flow it must carry the desired Ethernet header; for a layer 3 flow it must also carry the IP header and the UDP or TCP header fields. Not every field has to be identical to the real flow: the only requirement is that the flow entropy follows the same path, producing the same equal-cost path selection or multicast pruning behaviour. The network operator must be able to configure the flow entropy parameters on the switch from which a diagnostic is triggered.

One side effect needs care. Edge TRILL switches learn MAC address associations from the packets they see, and because the flow entropy field mimics real packets it could pollute that learning. TRILL OAM must therefore provide ways to prevent addresses being learned from the flow entropy field, for example by suppressing learning from OAM messages altogether. TRILL itself has no way to identify OAM messages, and the most reliable way to add one, without restricting the flow entropy field, is to change the TRILL header to carry an Alert flag. The header has two unused reserved bits, one of which could be used. The flag must not take part in equal-cost path hashing, and the solutions must not rely on it alone but on the flag together with the OAM Ethertype, so that the flag stays protocol agnostic. Because this changes the TRILL header it is not backward compatible, so solutions should also offer a method that works with existing switches.
sections.plainLanguage: A test packet has to look exactly like real traffic so that it takes the same path, but it also has to be recognisable as a test. The RFC gives the shape of the frame and explains how to spot it without breaking older switches.

sections.title: Finding Faults
sections.content:
Fault management comes in two flavours. Proactive functions are configured by the operator to run periodically with no time bound, or to trigger when a particular event occurs. On-demand functions are started by the operator, either once or for a set period, to investigate a defect.

The proactive detection function is the continuity check, which periodically monitors the reachability between the end points in an association by exchanging continuity check messages. Reachability may be monitored for a specified path, for all paths, or for a representative path. Because TRILL does not keep unicast and multicast paths congruent, the mechanism must be able to watch unicast paths independently of multicast paths, and where there are equal-cost paths it must be able to exercise them one at a time. The end points exchanging messages for a given monitored entity must use the same transmission period. The function has to detect loss of continuity to one or more remote end points, unexpected connectivity between isolated VLANs or labels, unexpected connectivity to one or more remote end points, and a mismatch of the transmission period between end points.

When a fault is found it is signalled in one of two ways. A forward defect indication signals a failure detected by a lower-layer mechanism and is transmitted away from the direction of the failure: in a chain of four switches where the middle link fails, the switch on the near side of the failure signals towards the far end and the other one signals the other way. It is used for alarm suppression, where one transport-level fault would otherwise raise a flood of service-level alarms, and for working with other layer protocols. A reverse defect indication signals that the sender has lost continuity and is transmitted in the direction of the failure, so that the far end learns about a one-way fault. Where equal-cost paths exist it must say which path the failure was found on. It allows an operator to look at one end point and deduce the health of the whole monitored entity.

On demand, the operator can run connectivity verification. It must be able to carry variable-length padding, to test connectivity problems caused by the maximum packet size, and test message formats as defined in the benchmarking methodology. For unicast the test starts at an end point and may target an intermediate point or another end point, either at network granularity over a test flow in a test VLAN or label, or at flow granularity over an operator-specified VLAN or label with operator-specified flow parameters. For multicast it tests every branch and leaf of a distribution tree, and needs ways to stop a storm of replies overwhelming the initiating switch, for example by staggering the replies with a random delay timer with a preset upper bound; multicast verification targets end points only and intermediate points are transparent to it. It must work for an un-pruned tree, where the operator supplies the tree identifier and a campus-wide diagnostic VLAN or label, and for a pruned tree, where the operator supplies the tree identifier and label, and optionally the IP multicast group.

Fault isolation traces the path of a flow hop by hop to localise a failure down to a port, link or node. Because TRILL does not require the forward and reverse paths to match, the operation is direction sensitive: given two switches, the fault has to be traced in both directions, and single-sided isolation is generally not possible. It should also work over distribution trees, both un-pruned and pruned.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two habits of monitoring. One runs all the time and shouts when something breaks; the other is run by hand when the operator wants to dig in. Because TRILL's paths are not symmetrical, digging in usually means doing it from both ends.

sections.title: Measuring Loss and Delay
sections.content:
Performance monitoring is optional, and can be run on a schedule or on demand; since the underlying functions are the same, the document does not distinguish between the two. Packet loss cannot be measured by counting user data packets, because TRILL gives multipoint-to-multipoint connectivity and a user packet can be delivered to more switches or ports than necessary, through broadcast, un-pruned multicast or unknown unicast flooding. A statistical estimate is needed instead, and the RFC's approach is to send synthetic OAM packets that are counted only by the ports that were supposed to receive them. The statistical considerations in the metro Ethernet forum's work on synthetic traffic should be followed, especially on how much synthetic traffic to generate and how that affects the accuracy of the loss count. The probes start at an end point and target an end point, and both one-way and two-way measurement are supported.

Packet delay is measured by putting timestamps in the OAM packets. To keep the measurement accurate, the position of the timestamp within the packet has to be fixed at a known offset so that hardware can do the timestamping, and hardware implementations must timestamp as close to the wire as they can. One-way and two-way measurement are again both supported. One-way measurement needs the clocks of the two switches to be synchronised; the round trip time does not, and the mechanisms for synchronising clocks between TRILL switches are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a real frame can be copied to more places than it should, counting real frames cannot tell you the loss rate. The RFC measures loss with its own test packets instead, and measures delay with timestamps placed where the hardware can read them.

sections.title: Configuration, Notifications and Security
sections.content:
TRILL switches may be configured for OAM through a command line, SNMP or NETCONF. To keep the plug-and-play character of TRILL, the number of parameters that have to be set should be as small as possible, and the mechanisms should lean on default values and on auto-discovery, using IS-IS where it applies. The domain parameters are a name, whose recommended default is the string DEFAULT, and a level that is an integer from 0 to 7 with a default of 0. The association parameters are a name, whose recommended default is the string vl or fgl followed by the VLAN or label identifier as a decimal number, for example vl42, and an optional list of end point identifiers. The end point parameters are an identifier, which the connectivity fault management standard limits to 1 to 8191 but this document recommends widening to 1 to 65535 so that the switch nickname can be used as the default, a direction that is either up or down, the associated interface, and the association the end point belongs to. The continuity check parameters include the transmission interval, the loss threshold, for which the recommended default is 3 consecutive missed messages, the VLAN or label and flow parameters, and a hop count. Connectivity verification and fault isolation take an operation timeout, whose recommended default is 5 seconds, a repeat count whose recommended default is 1, a hop count, and a choice of whether replies come back in band or out of band.

The OAM mechanisms should also raise notifications to the operator, for faults found by the proactive functions, for defect indications received, for logged security incidents on the message channel, and for protocol errors such as misconfiguration. These may be sent by SNMP, by syslog messages, or by any other standard management protocol that supports asynchronous notifications. When performance monitoring is used, the metrics end up in one of two places: with one-way measurement at the target switch, and with two-way measurement all of them at the source switch, with the source-to-target subset also at the target.

On security, TRILL OAM has to provide ways to stop a rogue device from flooding the network with OAM messages and so overloading the switches, which could interrupt the OAM service or in the extreme disrupt connectivity; control-plane policing combined with shaping or rate limiting can help. It may optionally authenticate that a message came from an appropriate end point. And it has to stop OAM packets leaking outside the TRILL network or outside their maintenance domain, which can be done by having the end points filter on the maintenance level of received packets. For general TRILL security, the RFC points to the base specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework tries to need very little configuration, because a monitoring system that has to be set up on every switch is one that will not be set up. It also insists the checks cannot be turned into a weapon against the network.

items.title: Continuity check
items.text: Periodic messages between end points that prove the path still works.

items.title: Forward defect indication
items.text: Signals a fault found below, sent away from the failure.

items.title: Reverse defect indication
items.text: Signals a lost connection, sent towards the failure.

items.title: Connectivity verification
items.text: An on-demand test of unicast or multicast reachability.

items.title: Fault isolation
items.text: Traces the path hop by hop to pin a fault to a port, link or node.
